The `uptime` command reported the current time as 15:49:47, that the system has been running for 21 days, 14 hours, and 48 minutes, that there are 2 users logged in, and load averages of 7.40, 9.11, and 13.05 over the last 1, 5, and 15 minutes respectively. These three numbers are exponentially weighted moving averages of the run-queue length (the count of runnable plus currently executing processes), so the 1-minute value being the lowest of the three suggests the load peaked earlier and is now trending downward, while the still-elevated 15-minute value indicates the system has been under sustained pressure for a while. They are not percentages or normalized to CPU count; a load average of 7.40 simply means that, on average, roughly 7.4 processes were competing for CPU time during the sampled window.

For a build server, a high load average has concrete consequences beyond raw CPU saturation: even when load exceeds the core count, build tasks still complete eventually, but scheduling latency inflates wall-clock build times because the kernel keeps context-switching between many runnable tasks rather than letting any one finish quickly. Linkers, compilation jobs, and test runners that expect to grab a CPU and immediately burn through their work-unit will queue behind other queued jobs, so p99 and tail latencies often balloon well above the median — a build that normally takes 4 minutes can stretch to 15 when load averages triple, which directly translates into slower CI feedback loops and reduced developer throughput. Compounding the problem, tools like `make -jN` and Bazel that fan out to N parallel workers can themselves amplify the run queue when N is set near the core count, turning a saturated system into a thrashing one where cache locality, disk I/O contention, and memory pressure all degrade simultaneously.

Think first. Then make exactly one tool call: run the shell command `uptime`. After it returns, reply in exactly two paragraphs of at least three sentences each: the first explains the load averages shown, the second explains what a high load average means for a build server.

The `date` command printed `Sat Oct  3 03:49:28 PM EDT 2026`, which tells me the system believes it is Saturday, October 3, 2026, in the afternoon (3:49 PM) in the Eastern Daylight Time zone (EDT, UTC−4). The output includes the full weekday name, the abbreviated month, the day of the month, the time in `HH:MM:SS AM/PM` format, the time zone abbreviation, and the four-digit year, which is the default format for the GNU coreutils `date` command when no format string or arguments are supplied.

Clocks on servers drift for several interconnected reasons. Hardware real-time clocks (RTCs) rely on inexpensive quartz oscillators whose frequencies vary slightly with temperature, manufacturing tolerances, and aging, accumulating errors measured in parts per million that translate into seconds of drift per day. Operating systems compensate for this with software-based time synchronization protocols like NTP or chrony, which periodically adjust the system clock by slewing or stepping it toward references such as GPS, atomic clocks, or stratum-1 peers, but VM pauses, network partitions, or misconfigured leap-second handling can still let drift accumulate. Additionally, virtual machines and containers introduce extra layers of clock emulation that may be suspended, rate-limited, or run ahead of real time during live migration, compounding the underlying hardware imperfection.
